title: China Rose (Hibiscus rosa-sinensis): Benefits, Uses and What Science Actually Says
excerpt: China rose (Hibiscus rosa-sinensis) is used for hair, skin and wellness. Here is what lab and animal research shows, what is unproven, and how to stay safe.
content:
Quick answer: China rose (Hibiscus rosa-sinensis) is a flowering shrub that people in India and across tropical Asia have used for generations in hair oils, skin packs and home remedies. Lab and animal studies suggest its flowers and leaves have antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial activity, and may help wounds heal. Human clinical evidence is still thin, so treat it as a promising traditional plant, not a proven medicine.

If you grew up in India, you probably know this flower as jaba, gudhal or shoe flower. It sits outside temples, in front yards and in almost every grandmother's hair oil recipe. In the US and UK it is better known as Chinese hibiscus, a houseplant with huge, showy blooms. Below, I go through what the plant is, how people use it, what research has found so far, and where the claims run ahead of the evidence.

What is China rose (Hibiscus rosa-sinensis)?

China rose is an evergreen flowering shrub in the mallow family, Malvaceae. Its scientific name is Hibiscus rosa-sinensis, and its common names include China rose, Chinese hibiscus and shoe flower. It likely comes from tropical Asia, though botanists are not certain of its exact origin, and today it grows across tropical and subtropical regions worldwide.

The flowers come in red, white, yellow, orange, pink and peach, often with a darker center and a long stalk of yellow pollen sticking out. Gardeners love it because it blooms for most of the year in warm climates and does well in pots.

Beyond its looks, the plant contains natural compounds that researchers find interesting. A 2025 review in Food Science & Nutrition lists anthocyanins, saponins, quercetin, kaempferol and anthraquinones among the bioactive compounds found in different parts of the plant (Raza et al., 2025, as of November 2026). Red petals tend to be richer in anthocyanins, the pigments that give them their deep color.

Which parts of the plant are used, and for what?

Different parts of China rose show up in different traditional preparations:

Plant partTraditional and research uses
FlowersHair oils, skin packs, antioxidant research
PetalsCosmetic and herbal preparations, natural color
LeavesHair masks and conditioners, skin preparations
RootsSome traditional herbal preparations
Flower extractsStudied for antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects

In many Indian homes, fresh flowers and leaves are boiled in coconut oil to make a hair oil, or ground into a paste with water or yogurt for a hair mask. The leaves turn slimy when crushed, and that mucilage is a big part of why people say it leaves hair soft.

What are the possible health benefits of China rose?

Most of the evidence below comes from lab experiments (test tubes and cell cultures) and animal studies. That matters, because results in a rat or a petri dish often do not carry over to people. With that in mind, here is what has been reported.

Antioxidant activity

Flower and leaf extracts contain flavonoids and other phenolic compounds that neutralize free radicals in lab tests. The 2025 review describes these compounds scavenging reactive oxygen and nitrogen species and shifting markers of oxidative stress in experimental models. Oxidative stress plays a role in aging and many chronic diseases, which is why this keeps getting studied.

Anti-inflammatory effects

Extracts have lowered inflammatory signals such as IL-6 and TNF-alpha in lab and animal studies, according to the same review. Nobody has shown yet that drinking or applying China rose reduces inflammation in people in a meaningful way.

Antimicrobial activity

In lab experiments, certain extracts slowed the growth of bacteria such as E. coli and S. aureus and fungi such as Aspergillus species. Results depend a lot on which part of the plant was used and how the extract was made, and some extracts showed no effect at all.

Wound healing

This is one of the better studied areas, though still only in animals. In a 2012 study in the Indian Journal of Pharmacology, researchers applied ointments containing 5% and 10% ethanolic China rose flower extract to wounds in Wistar rats. The treated wounds closed faster, formed more collagen and gained more strength than untreated wounds, and the authors reported better results than a standard nitrofurazone ointment (Bhaskar and Nithya, 2012, as of November 2026). Promising, but rats are not people, and you should never put homemade plant pastes on an open wound.

Blood sugar

Animal research suggests extracts may lower blood glucose, triglycerides and cholesterol. That sounds exciting if you or a family member has diabetes, but human evidence is not good enough to rely on. If you take diabetes medicine, adding an herbal extract on your own could push your sugar too low.

Liver protection

Some animal studies report that extracts reduced certain kinds of chemically induced liver damage. Again, this has not been confirmed in human trials.

Is China rose good for hair and skin?

Hair care is where China rose is most famous, especially in Ayurvedic and South Asian home remedies. People use it to condition hair, reduce dryness and care for the scalp. Several lab and rat studies have tested leaf and flower extracts for hair growth, and some reported longer hair or more follicles in treated animals. A 2024 review in the International Journal of Medical Studies proposes possible mechanisms, including effects on the hair growth phase and on an enzyme linked to hair loss, but those ideas still need testing in people.

A hibiscus oil or mask will likely make hair feel softer and look shinier, mostly thanks to the oil and the slippery mucilage. Whether it regrows hair in humans is unproven. If you are losing hair fast or in patches, see a dermatologist, because thyroid problems, low iron and hormonal changes are common causes that a flower cannot fix.

For skin, China rose shows up in soothing and moisturizing packs and in some commercial skincare. Its antioxidants make it a reasonable ingredient in a face pack. Do a patch test on your inner arm first, since any plant can cause irritation or allergy.

Is China rose the same as the hibiscus in hibiscus tea?

No, and this mix-up is very common. The deep red hibiscus tea sold in stores and cafes is usually made from Hibiscus sabdariffa, also called roselle. It is a different species. Roselle has more human clinical research, especially on blood pressure and metabolic health.

When you read that "hibiscus lowers blood pressure," that claim is mostly about roselle tea, not China rose. Keep the two apart when you read health articles, product labels or social media posts.

What else is China rose good for besides health?

  • In gardens, it brightens yards, balconies and parks with color most of the year in warm climates.
  • The flowers feed bees, butterflies and other pollinators.
  • Red hibiscus is offered in Hindu worship, especially to Goddess Kali and Lord Ganesha.
  • Cosmetic makers use it in herbal hair oils, shampoos and skincare.
  • The petals have been used to color food and to dye fabric.
  • Its compounds keep drawing interest from pharmaceutical and cosmetic scientists.

Is China rose safe? Precautions to know

Used on hair and skin, China rose is generally considered gentle. Taking it by mouth as medicine is a different story. The 2025 review notes that animal studies found it safe at doses between 400 and 800 mg per kg of body weight, but animal safety does not guarantee human safety, and long-term human trials are missing. Some older research has also reported anti-fertility effects in animals.

Follow these sensible precautions:

  • Do not eat large amounts of raw flowers, leaves or roots as a remedy.
  • Do not put plant extracts or pastes on open wounds without medical advice.
  • Herbal preparations can interact with medicines, especially for diabetes and blood pressure. Ask your doctor first.
  • If you are pregnant, trying to conceive or breastfeeding, talk to a healthcare professional before using any medicinal preparation.
  • Never replace prescribed medicine with an herbal remedy.
  • Patch test any homemade hair or skin product before using it widely.

So, is China rose worth using?

As a garden plant and a gentle hair and skin ingredient, yes. China rose has a long history, and early research gives some scientific backing to traditional uses like hair conditioning and wound care. As a medicine, not yet. Most of the exciting results come from lab and animal studies, and researchers themselves say long-term clinical trials are needed before anyone can call it a proven treatment.

If you enjoy a homemade hibiscus hair oil, keep using it. Just do not let a flower stand in for a doctor's advice.

This article is for general information and is not medical advice. Most benefits discussed come from laboratory experiments, animal studies or traditional use, and are not proven treatments for human diseases.

FAQ

What is China rose called in India?

It goes by many names, including jaba (Odia and Bengali), gudhal (Hindi), japa in Ayurveda, and shoe flower in English. Its scientific name is Hibiscus rosa-sinensis.

Can I drink China rose tea?

Some people do, but most hibiscus tea research is on a different plant, Hibiscus sabdariffa (roselle). China rose has little human research as a drink, so keep amounts small and check with a doctor if you are pregnant, take medicine or have a health condition.

Does China rose really help hair growth?

Lab and animal studies are encouraging, but there is no strong human evidence that it regrows hair. It can condition hair and make it feel softer. See a dermatologist for real hair loss.

How do I use China rose for hair at home?

A common method is to heat a few fresh flowers and leaves in coconut oil until they crisp, cool and strain the oil, then massage it into the scalp. Another is a paste of crushed leaves and flowers left on for about 20 to 30 minutes before washing. Patch test first.

Is China rose safe for children and pets?

Ask a pediatrician before using any herbal preparation on a child. For pets, check with your vet, and keep them from chewing large amounts of any garden plant.

Which color of China rose is best for remedies?

Traditional recipes usually call for the single-petaled red variety, and red petals contain more anthocyanins. There is no solid human evidence that one color works better than another.
